section.title: Design Considerations
section.p: All messages and user interface texts must be defined in resource bundles. The usual mechanisms can be used to load the desired localization. But we do not want to use strings references in the source code and so we should aim for applications with "no string references attached.". This approach allows refactoring with conventional tools and is brittle. All texts are defined through properties classes and instance variables. The variables are strings or arrays of strings. This approach was documented on the Java Net by Evan Summer. Utilities are provided to generate resource bundles, properties files and to verify that a translation provides all the definitions.

We introduce a phased approach for translating an application. First, we move strings into a message class. This is achieved by cutting and pasting strings out of application classes into the message class. Additionally, an existing resource bundle, as produced by IDE might be merged into the messages class, with the assistance of some trivial code generation. We recommend one class per major package to have clear grouping, scalable applications, and no class inflation.

This first phase enables us to ensure neat and consistent naming of the keys we use to reference messages. For example, we can readily rename the message keys using IDE refactorings, to correct spelling mistakes and inconsistent naming conventions.

The next phase is to generate the master resource bundle from the message class. We use reflection on the message class to generate the key/value pairs, which we cut and paste into the master resource bundle file. After this stage, the resource bundle can be translated into multiple languages.

At startup, the application loads the resource bundle for the current locale, and uses reflection to configure the message class from the resource bundle. This offers a mechanism to ensure that the resource bundle is consistent, ie. there are no strings that remain untranslated.
